newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: World labour leader says Seoul reputation at stake.
newsitem.headline: World labour leader says Seoul reputation at stake.

text.p: An international trade union leader, brushing aside threats of deportation, said on Monday South Korea's industrial crisis undermined the country's image and that its reputation was at stake over a new labour law.

Bill Jordan, head of the Brussels-based International Confederation of Free Trade Unions, was speaking after arriving in Seoul to lead a 10-member delegation in a fresh show of solidarity for unionists protesting against the controversial law.

Four world labour leaders, including a representative to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), left last Thursday after being threatened with deportation for appearing at strike-related news conferences and rallies. "World opinion is a factor in this issue because what is at stake is the reputation of Korea, not just its politics but its trading relations," Jordan said in a telephone interview.
"The events of the last two weeks have seriously undermined Korea's trade image as a reliable country and one with which you can do trade."

The OECD and other foreign labour groups have said the law, which was rammed through parliament on December 26, violates worker rights to freedom of expression by maintaining a ban on new union bodies until 2000. The law also allows companies to lay off workers and replace strikers.
Before fugitive leaders of the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions backed away on Saturday from calls for indefinite stoppages, the government had refused to yield any ground.

But in a reversal, President Kim Young-sam will meet opposition leaders on Tuesday to discuss the law and prosecutors are delaying the arrest of seven unionists holed up at Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral.
Jordan and his team later joined the confederation leaders at a news conference at the cathedral, where he urged all sides to engage in dialogue to solve the dispute.
Several delegates told reporters they believed they were followed after arriving at the airport and that security officials were shadowing their movements.
Authorities were not available to comment.
Jordan said he was not deterred by deportation threats.

"There is nothing that is going to stop me, one, speaking the truth about this present set of circumstances and, two, our prime purpose of coming here, together with showing solidarity, which is to see what we can do to resolve the situation," he said.
South Korea's top immigration official has said the delegation would be allowed in but warned it would be expelled if members joined strike-related protests.
The OECD, which South Korea officially joined last December, is holding a meeting on January 22 to review the law.
South Korea, which argues the law is necessary to boost international competitiveness, has said its partners in the OECD rich-nations club were powerless to change the legislation.
It took a dim view of the four world labour leaders last week, who attracted intense local media coverage with visits to Myongdong and by appearing as star guests at worker rallies.
The only legitimate union group in South Korea is the Federation of Korean Trade Unions.
Jordan said his team, most of whom are here for three days, would meet government officials but no details were available.
Key export industries were hit by more than three weeks of wildcat stoppages in protest at the law.
